outline.h2: Which user onboarding metrics point to a screen you can redesign?
outline.answerHint: **Six user onboarding metrics point to screens: sign-up completion, setup completion, step drop-off, time to value, activation rate and first-week retention, arranged as a tree under trial-to-paid conversion.**
points: Metrics tree (visual 1 + astext nested list). Explain reading direction: start at the root that moved, go down one level at a time, stop at the leaf that moved most.
Why trial-to-paid sits at the root but is not in the 6: it lags by the whole trial and mixes in pricing, sales and billing.
One sentence that a leaf is a stretch of screens, not a single metric owner; name the screens.
Bridge: 'A tree only works if every team computes each number the same way.'

outline.h2: How do the 6 user onboarding metrics compare, formula by formula?
outline.answerHint: **The 6 metrics differ in their denominator, their window and the two events they sit between, and those three choices decide whether a number can be compared from month to month.**
points: Comparison table (visual 2 + astext table; keywordCarrier.count6). Values from eav rows; activation and time to value link to the sibling for choosing the event (one link, not restated).
Onboarding completion vs activation: completing a checklist is not activation; one paragraph, answers PAA 'difference' question.
First-week retention vs the hub's day-7 return rate (one sentence).
Denominator trap: count users who started the step, not all sign-ups, for step metrics; count the whole sign-up cohort for activation.
Bridge: 'With six candidates on the table, the next decision is which three earn a place on the dashboard.'

outline.h2: How do HEART and goals-signals-metrics narrow user onboarding metrics to three?
outline.answerHint: **Google's HEART framework and its goals-signals-metrics process narrow the list: name the onboarding goal, pick the behavior that shows progress, and keep only the numbers that track that behavior.**
points: HEART 5 categories in one sentence; onboarding leans on Adoption, Task success and Retention (Google paper, GV article; Kerry Rodden named once).

Goals-Signals-Metrics worked for onboarding (eav example). Result: one outcome metric (activation rate), one speed metric (time to value), one quality metric (first-week retention); the other three become diagnostic drill-downs.
Happiness (NPS/CSAT) and support tickets as guardrails, asked after first value, not before (FAQ 5 expands).
Do not reuse ux-design-for-saas's 'at kick-off we usually settle on…' sentence.
Bridge: 'None of these numbers exists until the events behind them fire from every path.'

outline.h2: Which events does user onboarding analytics need first?
outline.answerHint: **User onboarding analytics needs one event per meaningful step, each carrying the same properties (role, plan, channel, platform and step index), plus a first-value event that fires from every path into it.**
points: Event spec table (data module 3; hypothetical event names).
Carrier sentence for 'in-app analytics for user onboarding' (keywordCarrier.secondary).
Paths that skip the UI (import, API, admin-created accounts) must still fire the event; one sentence and a plain-text pointer to the automation sibling's misfire example — do not retell it.
Open vs closed funnels in GA4 (eav, support.google.com link): use closed funnels for first-run setup, open for optional steps.
Tools in one line: Mixpanel, Amplitude, GA4 for funnels; Microsoft Clarity for session recordings (home.ts tools list). No ranking.
Bridge: 'Once the funnel is trustworthy, drop-off by step tells you where to look.'

outline.h2: Where does drop-off by step point to a screen to redesign?
outline.answerHint: **Drop-off by step points to the screen where the most users leave in absolute numbers, and the shape of the loss (one spike or a slow leak) tells you whether to fix one field or cut steps.**
points: Symptom → screen diagnosis map (visual 3 + astext table).
Absolute vs relative loss (eav step drop-off).

Analytics say where, not why: watch 10–20 session recordings of users who left at that step before choosing the fix — FLAG: '10–20' is method ('I watch…'), not a sourced figure; NN/g link for analytics vs research.
Regulated flows: link the KYC sibling's measurement section for ID retries and pending time; do not rebuild its table.
LEAD ANGLE 1 here (see leadAngle).
Bridge: 'Drop-off counts who leaves; time to value shows how long the ones who stay are kept waiting.'

outline.h2: What does time to value show that activation rate hides?
outline.answerHint: **Time to value shows how long activated users waited, and its slow tail exposes the screens that block on data, integrations or teammates even when activation rate looks healthy.**
points: Median plus 90th percentile plus share never reached (eav). Why not the average: a few multi-day accounts drag it.
Hypothetical histogram described in prose (no visual): two humps = two paths (sample data vs real import).
Screens the tail points to: empty states, import, integration connect, invite waits; link sibling's empty-state guidance only if not already linked (one sibling link per target rule).

TradeZella (DOWN link): 'Hard to learn. New users took long to get productive.' listed before the redesign; the whole web and mobile redesign later reported +25% retention. Do not attribute it to onboarding alone; do not reuse the sibling's 'No onboarding guide' sentence as the lead fact.
Bridge: 'Speed and reach still do not tell you whether first value stuck.'

outline.h2: How should you read activation rate and first-week retention together?
outline.answerHint: **Read activation and first-week retention as a 2×2: users who activate but do not return point to a weak activation event or second-session prompt, and users who return without activating point to setup or empty states.**
points: 2×2 quadrant (visual 4 + astext table). Quadrants: activated + returned (healthy), activated + not returned (event too shallow → sibling link to choosing the event, or second-session prompt), not activated + returned (interested but stuck → setup, empty state), neither (sign-up promise mismatch or wrong audience; check acquisition channel split).
Read by sign-up cohort, only after the 7-day window closes for the whole cohort.
Bridge: 'In a B2B product, each quadrant splits again by role.'

outline.h2: Which user onboarding metrics change for B2B admins and invited members?
outline.answerHint: **B2B user onboarding metrics split at two levels: workspace activation for the admin who set up the account and member activation for each invited user, plus the invite acceptance rate that connects them.**
points: Account vs user level (eav). Invite acceptance rate = invites accepted ÷ invites sent (method; excluded from the 6, named in count6).
Why a member's time to value should be shorter than the admin's (they skip setup); link the sibling's admin/member section instead of describing the paths.
SSO and domain-joined members: they never see sign-up, so leave them out of the sign-up completion denominator.
Bridge: 'Once the numbers point at a screen and you redesign it, you need proof the change worked.'

outline.h2: How do you prove a redesigned onboarding screen moved the number?
outline.answerHint: **Prove it with a concurrent A/B test or holdout on the redesigned screen where traffic allows, or with sign-up cohorts compared only after every user's activation window has closed.**
points: Before/after cohort pitfalls: channel mix, seasonality, pricing changes; read the same segment split as the baseline.

Concurrent comparison: redesigned screen vs current screen for randomly split new sign-ups; guardrails (support tickets, first-week retention) checked too. Link the automation sibling's holdout section for message rules; do NOT re-cite Braze or its 1–15% figure, do not rebuild its metric table.

No minimum sample number unless sourced; say 'small B2B trials rarely have the traffic for an A/B test, so a clean cohort read plus 5 to 8 interviews is the honest fallback' (interview count from the hub).
Hub fact: our release-and-measure week helps set up an A/B test where possible and compares activation before and after (UP link 2, fragment conditional).
LEAD ANGLE 2, then close with Ahmad's one-sentence first-person recommendation, no label, no 'Bottom line' H2.

faqs.q: How many user onboarding metrics should a dashboard show?
faqs.a: Three on the main view: activation rate, time to value and first-week retention. Keep sign-up completion, setup completion and step drop-off one click down as diagnostics, because they explain a change rather than measure success.

faqs.q: Is onboarding completion the same as activation?
faqs.a: No. Completion means a user finished your checklist or tour; activation means they reached the action that predicts they will stay. A user can tick every box and never get value, so track both and trust activation.

faqs.q: How are customer onboarding metrics different from user onboarding metrics?
faqs.a: Customer onboarding metrics track a people-led program, such as time from signed contract to go-live and kickoff-to-training time. User onboarding metrics track what each user does alone in the product. Link the sibling's user vs customer section (fragment conditional).

faqs.q: Which tools track user onboarding analytics?
faqs.a: Product analytics tools such as Mixpanel, Amplitude or Google Analytics 4 build the funnels; Microsoft Clarity adds session recordings that show why users leave. Onboarding tools such as Appcues, Userpilot or Pendo report on their own guides, not on your screens. No ranking, no pricing.

faqs.q: Should NPS or CSAT count as an onboarding metric?
faqs.a: Yes, as a guardrail, not a target. HEART files them under Happiness. Ask after the user reaches first value; a survey before it measures the sign-up form, not the product.

visuals.idea: Top-down tree: trial-to-paid conversion (gray, 'lagging') → activation rate and first-week retention → sign-up completion, setup completion (with step drop-off as a child), time to value → leaf chips naming screens (sign-up form, setup wizard, empty state + first task, invite flow, second-session prompt). A small 'read downward' arrow. Text panel: nested list.

6 horizontal cards, one per metric, each with formula, denominator, window, start → end event and a screen icon on the right. Not a plain grid table: card rows with a colored left edge per tree level. Text panel: the same table.

Left column: 6 small funnel-shape thumbnails showing the data pattern (one cliff, slow staircase, cliff after a plug icon, cliff at an envelope, phone-only cliff, cliff at a card icon). Arrows to the implicated screen and the first fix to test. Text panel: table pattern | screen | first fix | confirm with.

x = activated within window (no/yes), y = returned in first week (no/yes). Each quadrant: short name, what it means, which screen to open first. Not a decision matrix of automate/keep human (sibling) — label axes with the two metrics. Text panel: 4-row table.

Horizontal timeline of 3 weekly sign-up cohorts, each with its 7-day activation window shaded; a 'read here' marker placed only after the last window closes; a redesigned-screen release flag between cohort 1 and 2; a side lane showing a concurrent 50/50 split as the stronger option. Illustrative, no data. Not a two-curve lift chart (the automation sibling has one). Text panel: ordered steps.

CASE STUDY (exact facts only): TradeZella, content/case-studies/tradezella.md: problems listed before the redesign include 'Hard to learn. New users took long to get productive.' and 'No onboarding guide. First-time traders had nothing to walk them through setup.' Results of the whole web and mobile redesign (dashboard analytics as the main focus): +40% user interaction, +25% user retention, +30% new customers. Never attribute a result to onboarding or to metrics work. No case study lists this hub; do not call TradeZella an onboarding project.

CONFLICT (terminology, low risk): the hub names 'day-7 return rate' without defining it (saas-onboarding defines it as a session on day 7, counting the sign-up day as day 1); this post's sixth metric is 'first-week retention' (a session on days 2–7).
